prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, rooted in his poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical project.

statement.case_for: My preferred candidate is unchanged: Cărtărescu, one writer in one prize part. I reached that after testing the case against the reservations raised in round 1 and the chair's questions, not because the files are parallel. The literary case, as I understand it from public knowledge and not from independent verification, is a voice that is immediately recognisable, with long, patterned sentences. It is carried through very large structures, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding) and Solenoid. In them memory, the body and cosmology form one imaginative and intellectual project, and the work is not topical. That is a harder test than one well-made book, and it is the reason I put him first on whole-oeuvre grounds. On the chair's citation question I now side with prose as the load-bearing element and poetry as the formative ground. My round-1 wording named the poetry of his beginnings, but corpus coverage in translation is too thin for a citation to treat the poetry as an independently assessed body of work. The revised wording keeps the Romanian language and the project (memory, body, dream, metaphysical architecture) and avoids any regional or period label. On Nobel's 'idealistic tendency', I do not think the phrase separates Cărtărescu from Carson or Wright. It is a contested phrase, and I would read it as an orientation toward large questions about human existence, which a metaphysical prose project can meet. I would not use it to settle the ranking. I see no reservation strong enough to prefer P000 or another ballot. The reservations are real, but they concern how fully the case can be tested, not a failure of a stated criterion.
statement.case_against: The reservations I keep are the shared ones, and I do not think the exchange resolved them. First, the language-level achievement (rhythm, syntax, sonic patterning) cannot be judged by me directly, so a recommendation rests on translation. Second, whether the late, very long novels extend the early project or partly repeat it is still open. Members who say the recurring images show that length is structural may be right, but that is an inference about design, not a close reading, and it does not exclude unevenness within books. Third, my knowledge of the poetry, early prose and essays is thinner than my knowledge of the large novels, so a whole-oeuvre citation rests on partial coverage. If close reading of the late volumes showed repetition and not development, the sustained-quality criterion would weaken and the choice among alternatives would need to be reopened.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu to first place in round 1 and ranks Carson second. He reads the repeated images across the trilogy and Solenoid as showing that length is structural. He proposes that any Carson citation rest on her written lyric and essay work, with visual form as support.
responses.response: I accept his proposal as the fairest way to frame a Carson citation, and it is a real narrowing. On that basis the question is whether the written lyric and essay corpus carries sustained quality across the oeuvre. I cannot answer that confidently from public knowledge. I did not rank her in my opening list, and the exchange has made me take her more seriously than I did, so I would not call her case weak. It still depends on a few celebrated hybrid works, and the weight of translations as authorship still has to be decided in a citation. I part from him slightly on his structural reading of Cărtărescu's length. I find it plausible, but I treat it as a hypothesis to test against the whole corpus, not as settled.

responses.point: Carlberg did not place Murnane in her top eight. She asks what I see in his late works that widens the range beyond the procedure of the earlier ones, and says that is the point on which her view could move.
responses.response: I owe a direct answer and it is a concession. From public knowledge I cannot show that Murnane's later works widen his range. What I can say is that they deepen and concentrate the same system of landscape, memory and mental images, with a very consistent syntax. That is formal integrity, but it is not the same as breadth. Her question exposes the weakest point of my second alternative, and I will not claim more than I can support. The narrowness is by design and not a defect, but it makes the significance-across-the-body-of-work criterion harder to meet than for a writer whose project grows in scale. I keep him as an alternative because the voice is singular, not because I can show development.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Murnane fifth and questions whether a deliberately closed method yields enough variety over a corpus. She also asks the committee not to treat scale as automatically a virtue, and she says my caution about uneven quality in very long books applies to Cărtărescu too.
responses.response: She is right that scale is not a virtue in itself, and I cannot claim the late Cărtărescu volumes are even. That is why I put the pattern-versus-overextension question in my reservations and do not treat length as proof. The distinction I would hold is that scale becomes evidence when it carries development, as the trilogy and Solenoid appear to do, and it is neutral or negative when it only repeats. For Murnane the equivalent test is variety within a closed method. I agree that neither writer can be settled from an overview. Where I differ is that the growth of the imaginative architecture gives me a testable claim on Cărtărescu, whereas for Murnane the claim is about intensity of method.

responses.point: Palm finds Murnane's significance harder to establish because his project is deliberately narrow and his international reception is late and less tested. She notes that a milder version of the range concern applies to Cărtărescu, whose work spans poetry and several large prose works.
responses.response: I accept that late reception counts for little in itself, since reception is not literary merit. The substantive issue is range, and there I largely agree with her. Her point that a milder version applies to Cărtărescu is fair, and I would say so in the citation by anchoring it in the prose project and not claiming more breadth than the translated corpus can support. I also take her view that if the committee judged by best individual books, the comparison with Carson would tighten. That is a question about what the prize assesses, and I read the whole-oeuvre criterion as asking for sustained architecture, which favours Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sward suggests framing the citation around the prose, with poetry named cautiously as formative ground. She also says the exchange moved her toward treating Wright as a closer alternative, while she finds the evidence of a deepening vision across a long career stronger for Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I now follow her on the citation, and I have changed my wording accordingly: prose as the load-bearing element, with poetry as its root. On Wright, I agree that the novels' scale and invented idiom are a real formal achievement and that she should not be read mainly through political symbolism. I keep Michon and Murnane, not Wright, as my alternatives because of my own opening ranking, and I do not claim that ordering is more than a judgment under uncertainty. Her point about deepening vision across a long career is the strongest argument against treating a small number of very large books as equivalent evidence.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's sentence-level density, rhythm and sonic patterning survives in translation remains unresolved. My judgment rests on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, not on independent verification of the Romanian texts or translated editions.

Whether the late, very long novels extend the early project or partly repeat it is not settled by the supplied evidence. Naming the strongest and weakest volumes on this question would need close reading of the whole corpus, which I cannot supply.

Coverage of the poetry, early prose and essays is thinner than coverage of the large novels, so whether poetry belongs in the citation as a co-equal element or as formative ground is a judgment under uncertainty.

For the alternatives, Murnane's narrow range, which I cannot show to widen, and Michon's small corpus and French-dependent style both bear on the whole-oeuvre criterion and are unresolved. My comparison with Carson's written lyric and essay corpus is thin.
Whether Nobel's 'idealistic tendency' discriminates among the shortlisted writers is contested, and I have not treated it as deciding the ranking.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or translation connection to any shortlisted writer. I disclose for transparency that I write historical fiction about Central Europe and that I have been a critic at Dagens Nyheter since 2008. The profile does not say whether any of my criticism there concerns a shortlisted writer, so I cannot rule that out from the supplied evidence. My literary practice is context, not a reason to favour any candidate, and I do not want the citation to read Cărtărescu as a regional figure. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
